traits.note: Mabberley's Plant-book (4th ed., 2017), under the genus (Palmae III 4b): massive palms with bisexual flowers and palmate leaves on spiny petioles.

traits.leaf_division.note: Mabberley's Plant-book (4th ed., 2017), under Palmae, subfamily III Coryphoideae: leaves induplicately palmate in all but Phoenix and the Caryoteae (Arenga, Caryota, Wallichia), which are pinnate. A fan palm's blade is one piece cut into segments: simple, parted, palmate.

traits.leaf_incision.note: Mabberley's Plant-book (4th ed., 2017), under Palmae, subfamily III Coryphoideae: leaves induplicately palmate in all but Phoenix and the Caryoteae (Arenga, Caryota, Wallichia), which are pinnate. A fan palm's blade is one piece cut into segments: simple, parted, palmate.

traits.division_pattern.note: Mabberley's Plant-book (4th ed., 2017), under Palmae, subfamily III Coryphoideae: leaves induplicately palmate in all but Phoenix and the Caryoteae (Arenga, Caryota, Wallichia), which are pinnate. A fan palm's blade is one piece cut into segments: simple, parted, palmate.

traits.fan_split_depth.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 285): the blade divided irregularly to about a third of its length into single-fold segments; Sargent (1922, p. 104) has it divided nearly to the middle. Read as a third to a half.

traits.segment_posture.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 285): the segments pendulous at maturity; Sargent (1922, p. 104): recurved.

traits.segment_filaments.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 285): the segments filamentous at their tips, the interfold filaments conspicuous; Sargent (1922, p. 104): the segments separate on their margins into numerous slender pale fibres.

traits.petiole_armature.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 285): the petiole strongly armed with curved teeth; Sargent (1922, p. 104): broad, thin, large and small, straight or hooked spines.

traits.petiole_tooth_form.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 285): curved teeth.

traits.petiole_teeth_distal.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 285): the teeth becoming smaller and sparser toward the blade.

traits.petiole_tooth_length_m.note: Neither flora gives the teeth's size: one to two and a half centimetres, set by eye from general knowledge of the genus, to be checked against measurements.

traits.petiole_tooth_spacing_m.note: Neither flora gives how far apart the teeth stand: about 3.5 cm on average, set by eye, to be checked against measurements.

traits.petiole_tooth_colour.note: Sargent (1922, p. 104): the spines confluent into a thin bright orange-coloured cartilaginous margin; the shade by eye.

traits.dead_leaf_colour.note: Sargent (1922, p. 105): a thick thatch of dead pendant leaves; its colour, a straw grey-brown, by eye from general knowledge of the genus, as the floras give none (a paler straw drew the thatch near white in the sun).

traits.clonal.note: Dransfield et al. (Genera Palmarum, 2nd ed., 2008), under the genus: its stems are solitary; its fan leaves are strongly costapalmate, the petiole running on into the blade as a rib; its dead leaves stay on the stem (marcescent) rather than falling cleanly.

generator.params.costa.why: The rib the fan's segments rise from, as a share of the frond: a fifth for a strongly costapalmate fan, a tenth for a shortly costapalmate one (the built-in cabbage and California fan palms, 0.18 and 0.12).

generator.params.skirt.why: Dead fronds hang on the stem instead of falling.

generator.params.dead_life.why: How many years a dead frond hangs, set by eye: the book says only that they stay on, and most such palms shed them within a few years (the California fan palm, whose skirt lasts for decades, sets its own).

generator.params.dead_angle.why: A dead frond hangs close against the stem, as the built-in California fan palm's do.

rules.note: Dransfield et al. (Genera Palmarum, 2nd ed., 2008), under the genus: its stems are solitary; its fan leaves are strongly costapalmate, the petiole running on into the blade as a rib; its dead leaves stay on the stem (marcescent) rather than falling cleanly.

appearance.note: Sargent (1922, p. 104-105): a thick thatch of dead pendant leaves descending from the crown, so a dead fan is drawn hanging closed, its segments falling together below its petiole (a narrow palmate card, its lobes spread a third as wide as a living fan's), its colour the dead leaves' (the family's rule).
